clue.text: Silly me, sure a fiddle featured in opera

indicators.note: silly letters are foolish and muddled, so the words that follow get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone scolds themselves for being sure that a fiddle appeared in an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' signals the anagram of all of ME SURE A FIDDLE; 'featured in' only links the fodder to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Strauss II's comic operetta about a masked ball, whose German title means The Bat.

clue.text: Tiny Tim's first single, oddly playing around America right now

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit around the abbreviation, holding it inside them
the letters are playing about, so they are rearranged
first here takes only the opening letter of the name Tim
oddly keeps the first, third and fifth letters of the word single

explanation.surface: A music critic notes that Tiny Tim's debut single is playing strangely all over America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'single' looks like the record but only lends its odd letters; 'playing' makes INSTNTLY, which goes 'around' A. A for America is rare outside USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean at this very moment, without any delay; a plain synonym.

clue.text: Where Puck gets a lot of stick, stalking female sculptor

indicators.note: the rink follows behind the female, as a stalker follows a target

parts.words: Where Puck gets a lot of stick
parts.note: an ice rink is where a hockey puck gets hit by sticks; the setter's pseudonym is Puck

explanation.surface: The setter Puck complains of taking criticism while pursuing a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Puck is this setter's name, so 'gets a lot of stick' reads as criticism, but here it is the ice-hockey puck on a rink.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Elisabeth Frink was an English sculptor known for bronze horses and figures.

clue.text: Saving money excited holding company

indicators.note: the jumbled letters hold the company abbreviation inside them
excited letters are agitated and stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled about money keeps it invested in a firm to save.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' gives ENOMY, and 'holding' wraps it round the company abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrift, cutting spending to keep money, is called making an economy; a synonym.

clue.text: Muesli, a little yogurt, nuts — heaven!

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters are scrambled
a little of the word yogurt is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A breakfast of muesli, a bit of yogurt and nuts is pure bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' looks like part of the breakfast but signals the anagram of MUESLI plus Y.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Elysian Fields were the paradise of the blessed dead, so the word means paradise.

clue.text: Plant herb, not rose, around ravine

indicators.note: the shortened herb goes around the ravine word, split either side of it
not means the flower name is removed from the herb

parts.note: rosemary is a culinary herb
taken as written, the letters removed from the herb
a chine is a deep narrow ravine, a word used on the Isle of Wight and in Dorset

explanation.surface: A gardening instruction: plant a herb other than a rose near a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' leaves MARY, which goes 'around' the ravine word; 'Plant' is factory equipment, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Plant in the industrial sense is the heavy equipment of a factory, a synonym for its engines and apparatus.

clue.text: 17 stuck halfway through Paul, Tramp, Vlad, even Rufus? Yes, initially

indicators.note: the letters wanted are lodged in the middle of the two names, straddling the comma

explanation.surface: A list of names, Paul, Tramp, Vlad and Rufus, with someone confirming an acrostic.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letters of 'Vlad, even Rufus? Yes' spell VERY, a second meaning of the answer, signalled by 'initially'. The definition is only the cross-reference to 17, the fanatic.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is a person with extreme views, the same sense as the fanatic answer to 17.

clue.text: More work required on song that's included with German opera

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: Utopia is the famous book by Sir Thomas More

indicators.note: the German word is included inside the song

parts.note: a lied is a German art song
mit is the German for with

explanation.surface: A composer needs more work on a song that goes with a German opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More' looks like 'additional' but is Sir Thomas More. Utopia Limited is a late Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera of 1893, one of their less-performed works.

clue.text: Bass has warning about fish in opera

indicators.note: the warning word goes about the single letter, enclosing it

parts.note: an alert is a warning
B is the abbreviation for bass in music
the herring is a common sea fish

explanation.surface: A bass fish comes with a warning about another fish in some opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bass' reads as the fish, alongside 'fish', but here it is the singing voice, B.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Britten's comic chamber opera about a shy young man crowned May King.

clue.text: Cross capital, say, to give evidence

indicators.note: say tells us to pronounce the phrase and hear what it resembles

parts.note: cross means testy, irritable; capital is money, wealth for investment

explanation.surface: A city, the capital, is told to cross over and testify in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross capital' looks like an instruction about a city, but it is TESTY MONEY spoken quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness's sworn statement in court is their evidence; the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Court summons gangster caught having sex earlier

indicators.note: earlier puts the gangster at the end, after the other pieces come first

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
it is a coy word for sex or sex appeal
Al Capone, the Chicago gangster, gives the name Al

explanation.surface: A mobster arrested for an earlier sex offence is summoned to court.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic legal word for a citation, the summoning of someone to appear before a judge.

clue.text: Strategy No 11 for an idiot

parts.note: a plan is a strategy
K is the eleventh letter of the alphabet, so strategy number 11 is plan K, after plan A

explanation.surface: A desperate list of strategies has reached number 11, fit only for a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 11' tempts a look at clue 11, but it is the alphabet's eleventh letter, extending the idea of Plan A.
explanation.definitionFit: Plank is British slang for a stupid person, thick as a plank of wood.

clue.text: Found one soldier in elaborately decorated housing

indicators.note: the decorated word houses the two short pieces inside it

parts.note: ornate means elaborately decorated
I is the Roman numeral for one
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier is discovered inside a fancy house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as discovered, but it is the verb meaning establish.
explanation.definitionFit: To found something is to establish or start it, the same as bringing it into being.

clue.text: Doctor pays out to this examining body?

definitions.note: a phrase naming the act of examining a corpse, a noun phrase like the answer

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor is paid for performing a post-mortem examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the person who does the examining but is the anagram signal; 'examining body' looks like a board of examiners.
explanation.definitionFit: A post-mortem is the medical inspection of a corpse to find the cause of death.

clue.text: Murder, with bad language beforehand

indicators.note: the language comes first, before the other piece

parts.note: Polish is the language of Poland
food that is off has gone bad

explanation.surface: A killing preceded by a stream of swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad language' reads as swearing, but the two words belong to different pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish someone off is slang for killing them, finishing them off.

clue.text: Nuts about you, said film star

indicators.note: the nuts word goes about the sheep word, enclosing it

parts.note: mast is the fallen nuts of beech and oak trees, used as animal feed

indicators.note: said tells us the word you is pronounced, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: the word you, spoken, sounds like a female sheep

explanation.surface: Someone declares they are crazy about you, said the movie star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts about you' reads as a declaration of love; nuts is the noun, beech mast.
explanation.definitionFit: The American actress of 1930s Hollywood, famous for innuendo-laden one-liners.

clue.text: Setter, I'm cross about 7

indicators.note: about means around and round about, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: a cross is the letter X

explanation.surface: The setter admits being angry about clue 7.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' reads as angry, but it is the X shape added to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Clue 7's answer means a fanatic with extreme views, the same as a radical zealot.

clue.text: Heavenly choir's first seen after DIY mishap leads to bad back

indicators.note: the choir's initial is placed after the other pieces
a mishap is an accident, so the letters are knocked out of order
back means the word for bad is read backwards

parts.note: ill means bad, as in ill effects

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of the word choir

explanation.surface: A do-it-yourself accident leaves someone with a bad back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mishap' turns DIY into IDY, and 'back' reverses ILL to LLI.
explanation.definitionFit: Idyllic means perfectly peaceful and charming, a near-synonym for blissful or paradisal.

clue.text: A newly invented word, eg acoge?

parts.note: the made-up word shows the letters CO sitting in the word AGE

explanation.surface: A newly made-up word is offered, with a nonsense example.
explanation.walkthrough: The nonsense word is itself an example of the definition, and it pictures CO in AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A coinage is a newly minted word or phrase, the noun from coining a term.

clue.text: Provision for baby agreed during brief correspondence

indicators.note: the agreement word goes during, that is inside, the shortened letter
brief means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a letter is a piece of correspondence
ay, or aye, is a word of agreement

explanation.surface: An arrangement for a baby is agreed in a short exchange of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brief' cuts LETTER to LETTE, which AY goes into.
explanation.definitionFit: A layette is the set of clothes and bedding prepared for a newborn.

clue.text: Book by author with no energy blockages

parts.note: a log is a book in which records are kept

indicators.note: with no means the energy symbol is taken out

parts.note: Henry James is the American-born novelist
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A book by a writer who has lost all energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes E from JAMES to leave JAMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Logjams are obstructions, originally of floating timber, now of any stuck traffic or process.

clue.text: Absorbing content from singer-songwriter

indicators.note: the content of a word is what lies inside it, leaving out its outer letters

parts.note: Sting is the English musician who wrote many of the Police's songs

explanation.surface: Taking in the work of a singer-songwriter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singer-songwriter' looks like one description of a person, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking food or drink into the body, swallowing it, is the sense of absorbing here.

clue.text: Brilliance of one of Elgar's Variations

indicators.note: a variation alters the arrangement, so the letters are reordered; also the Enigma Variations

explanation.surface: Praise for the brilliance of one of Elgar's Enigma Variations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variations' recalls Elgar's Enigma Variations but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A glare is a dazzling, harsh brightness of light.

clue.text: Tips off cruel schoolmaster? That's odd

indicators.note: taking the tips off removes the first and last letters

parts.note: Wackford Squeers is the brutal headmaster in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby

explanation.surface: Someone warns a harsh schoolmaster, finding something odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips off' reads as warns, but it removes the outer letters of SQUEERS, the cruel schoolmaster of Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Queer in its older sense means strange or peculiar.

clue.text: Having no starter, drink Scotch

indicators.note: with no starter the drink loses its opening letter

parts.note: squash is a fruit cordial diluted with water, a British soft drink

explanation.surface: Skipping the first course and going straight to a whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' and 'drink' suggest whisky, but Scotch is the verb meaning put an end to.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour or plan is to put an end to it, to suppress it.

clue.text: Love rat often providing inspiration for poet

indicators.note: the words provide, that is supply, the letters from within them

explanation.surface: An unfaithful lover often gives a poet material.
explanation.walkthrough: Erato is the Greek Muse of love poetry, apt given 'Love'.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry, one of the nine who inspire artists.

clue.text: A choreographer's entertaining friend that's French statesman

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: Rudolf Laban was a dance theorist and choreographer
ami is the French for friend

explanation.surface: A dancer's French friend turns out to be a statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'statesman' reads as a politician, but here it is a man from a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the US state of Alabama is a man of that state, a punning sense.

clue.text: Führer's edict ruined unknown opera

indicators.note: ruined letters are wrecked and remade in another order

parts.note: Z is an algebraic unknown, as are X and Y

explanation.surface: A dictator's decree wrecked an obscure opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unknown' qualifies the opera in the surface but gives Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Weber's German Romantic opera of 1821, The Freeshooter.
